Let
\[
\begin{aligned}
C_4&=h_2^2+4e_2f_2,\\
C_3&=2h_1h_2+4e_1f_2+4e_2f_1,\\
C_2&=h_1^2+2h_0h_2+4e_1f_1+4e_0f_2+4e_2f_0-6h_2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{Z\!\left(U(\mathfrak g)\right)=k[C_2,C_3,C_4].}
\]

Equivalently, without choosing an ordering for the noncommuting products,
\[
\begin{aligned}
C_2={}&h_1^2+2h_0h_2
+2(e_1f_1+f_1e_1)
+2(e_0f_2+f_2e_0)
+2(e_2f_0+f_0e_2),\\
C_3={}&2h_1h_2+4e_1f_2+4e_2f_1,\\
C_4={}&h_2^2+4e_2f_2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The displayed PBW-ordered form of \(C_2\) uses
\[
2(e_1f_1+f_1e_1)=4e_1f_1-2h_2,
\]
and similarly for \(e_0f_2\) and \(e_2f_0\), giving the correction \(-6h_2\).

To see why these are the generators, pass to the PBW associated graded algebra
\[
\operatorname{gr} U(\mathfrak g)\cong S(\mathfrak g).
\]
The Poisson center \(S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g}\) is generated by the top three coefficients of
\[
(h_0+h_1t+h_2t^2)^2+4(e_0+e_1t+e_2t^2)(f_0+f_1t+f_2t^2),
\]
namely
\[
\begin{aligned}
q_2&=h_1^2+2h_0h_2+4(e_1f_1+e_0f_2+e_2f_0),\\
q_3&=2h_1h_2+4(e_1f_2+e_2f_1),\\
q_4&=h_2^2+4e_2f_2.
\end{aligned}
\]
These are algebraically independent. Their PBW symmetrizations are exactly \(C_2,C_3,C_4\), and symmetrization sends invariant quadratic tensors to central elements of \(U(\mathfrak g)\). Hence \(C_2,C_3,C_4\in Z(R)\).

Conversely, if \(z\in Z(R)\), then its leading PBW symbol lies in \(S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g}=k[q_2,q_3,q_4]\). Subtracting the corresponding polynomial in \(C_2,C_3,C_4\) lowers the PBW degree, and induction gives \(z\in k[C_2,C_3,C_4]\). Thus no further central generators occur.
